title: The Last Straw(man)
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Brien, a self-described science-of-learning teacher, lists ten strawman arguments commonly aimed at explicit instruction and rebuts each in turn. He argues that explicit teaching does build critical thinking, because background knowledge is what students think with, and that practice is a fight against forgetting rather than drill and kill. He distinguishes explicit instruction from lecturing and from death by PowerPoint by pointing to chunking, constant checks for understanding and cognitive-load management. On groups, he cites social loafing and favours think-pair-share; on fun, he is sharply critical of gamified quiz tools such as Kahoot and Blooket. He closes by claiming that explicit teaching builds wellbeing through success and is well suited to project work when it is broken into sequenced steps.
points: Explicit instruction teaches critical thinking by supplying the base knowledge that complex problem solving depends on, then removing scaffolds.
Repeated practice and questioning is justified as the battle against forgetting, not drill and kill.
Explicit teaching is chunked, sequenced and checked constantly, which distinguishes it from lecturing and from slide-reading.
Social loafing evidence supports short pair-based talk over extended group work.
Gamified quizzes offer the illusion of fun and can inflate inequity, whereas rapport and story make lessons lively without being the point.
quotes: I am a teacher who prides themselves on wanting to defeat the research-implementation gap by engaging with evidence and using said evidence to inform my practice. This is completed with the aim not to achieve some mythical, undeniable best practice which is indisputable for the rest of our time on this planet but to implement the best practice as it stands right now.

In explicit instruction we do teach students to think critically, however we provide them with the base knowledge and skills they require sequentially in chunks until they are able to call on their base knowledge to solve complex problems which have been modelled to them before gradually removing the scaffolds.

There’s a range of studies which show that students with a strong base knowledge of a topic will often outperform students with stronger reading and writing skills. This is because without the knowledge to think with, how can you possibly comprehend and problem solve?

Basic knowledge and skills of literacy, numeracy, civics and history are timeless and empower our students to engage in society in an informed manner. Let us not bring in a generation who asks ChatGPT who they should vote for!

In reality if you came into one of my classes, you would see constant questioning of the students and often asking the same questions again and again. Sometimes in the same lesson, sometimes over a series of lessons.

By design explicit instruction breaks down information into small chunks and then sequences them carefully with checks for understanding relentlessly along the way. I don’t know what lectures were like for you at University or College, but my lecturers rarely took a breath in a 3 hour class let alone took time to make sure the audience understood.

Social loafing is a phenomenon where individuals in a group collectively put in less effort as they know other members of the group will pick up the slack. Studies have shown in a tug of war scenario that a group of people will collectively put in around 75% of the effort they would put in if they were doing it independently.
